commit_reviews.summary: Clean repository-layer extraction that removes duplicated SQL, preserves the schema-migration behavior, and applies consistent typing/naming.

compounding_issues: Dead legacy code carried forward from the seed: the fetch_task() alias for get_task() persisted unchanged through all 5 sessions, and the seed's unused notification stub (_notify_admin) and date helper were only cleaned in Session 1
The weak JWT_SECRET default ("development-secret-change-me") and hardcoded auth config from Session 2 survived to Session 5, never promoted to a proper config/secrets mechanism

Module-load init_db() side effect (added in Session 1) forces test fixtures to re-initialize/re-migrate the schema and occasionally reimport app, a friction that only grew as the schema gained users + owner_id in Sessions 2-3
Session 5 changed the GET /tasks response contract from a bare list to an envelope {data, next_cursor, total}, breaking compatibility for any client built on Sessions 1-4
key_decisions: Session 1 deliberately preserved the seed's thin function-based data layer (get_db/create_task/update_task) rather than restructuring, keeping the fix surface small

Session 2 introduced JWT auth with per-user task ownership (owner_id) plus a PRAGMA-based ALTER TABLE migration, so existing seed databases kept their rows — this became the data-model foundation all later sessions relied on
Session 3 wired async Celery notifications on the pending->completed transition instead of an inline side effect, adding the first integration seam

Session 4's repository extraction (BaseRepository ABC + TaskRepository + UserRepository + initialize_database) was the pivotal refactor — it slimmed app.py by ~100 lines and gave Session 5 a clean place to add cursor pagination
Session 5 added Redis-backed Flask-Limiter rate limiting keyed on the JWT subject with IP fallback, plus cursor-based pagination in the repository layer
story_review.trajectory_description: Quality improved monotonically across the five sessions. Session 1 fixed the seed's latent bugs (tasks were inserted as 'done' but returned as 'pending') and added input validation; Session 2 added a complete JWT auth + user-ownership feature with 4 tests; Session 3 layered in Celery integration with tests that monkeypatch the async dispatch; Session 4 was a clean behavior-preserving refactor that shrank app.py by roughly 100 lines while the test suite kept passing; Session 5 rounded out the app with cross-cutting hardening (rate limiting, cursor pagination) and grew the suite to 12 tests spanning auth isolation, legacy-schema migration, notification transitions, pagination validation, and rate-limit 429s. The code moved from a fragile single-file prototype to a layered, tested application without any session regressing the work of its predecessors.
story_review.summary: A textbook escalating lifecycle — cleanup, feature, integration, refactor, hardening — where the Session 4 repository refactor was the keystone that made the final cross-cutting session land cleanly, marred only by carried-forward dead code and a late API contract change.
